Lip balm not working? Here’s what you might be missing
item.description:
Even before winter fully sets in, many people are finding their lips dry, peeling, or cracked at the corners. Besides the change in weather, frequent lip licking, dehydration, and the use of certain cosmetics can also play a role. Doctors say it is important to start caring for your lips now rather than waiting for winter.
The skin on the lips is much thinner than on other parts of the face, and it has almost no oil-producing glands. As a result, lips lose moisture very easily. Without proper care, this dryness can lead to cracks, pain, and a burning sensation.
Change in weather: Falling humidity, dry air, and temperature fluctuations reduce the natural moisture of the lips. This is why many people’s lips start cracking even before winter arrives.
Frequent lip licking: When lips feel dry, many people wet them with their tongue. But once the saliva evaporates, the lips become even rougher, worsening cracks and discomfort.
Dehydration: Without enough water in the body, the lips and other parts of the face can become dry. However, chapped lips alone cannot confirm dehydration.
Cosmetics and toothpaste: Ingredients in some lipsticks, lip balms, scented cosmetics, and toothpastes can cause allergies or inflammation on the lips. If burning or dryness increases after using such products, they should be avoided.
Nutritional deficiencies: Lip problems, especially cracks at the corners of the mouth, can be linked to a lack of essential nutrients, including iron and vitamin B12. However, it would be wrong to conclude that someone has a deficiency based on these symptoms alone.
Skin conditions or infections: Lips that stay cracked for a long time, turn red, itch, or develop sores at the corners may also be affected by eczema, allergies, or infections.
Use lip balm regularly: Fragrance-free and flavor-free petroleum jelly or a plain lip balm can help lock in moisture. Applying it when lips feel dry and before bed may help.
Stop licking lips and picking at dry skin: Wetting the lips with the tongue and pulling off dry skin can cause wounds on the lip skin and increase burning.
Drink enough water: Drink water regularly according to your body’s needs. However, drinking water alone does not cure dry lips; keeping moisture in from the outside is also important.
Protect from the sun: Ultraviolet rays from the sun can damage the lips. When going out, a broad-spectrum lip balm with SPF 30 or higher can be used. If you stay outdoors for a long time, reapply it according to the product’s instructions.
Avoid irritating products: Products containing menthol, camphor, fragrance, or other harsh ingredients can worsen discomfort. If a product causes burning or dryness, stop using it.
Consult a doctor if the cracks do not improve despite basic care, if the problem persists, or if you develop severe pain, inflammation, sores, or signs of infection. If cracks at the corners of the lips keep recurring, it is especially important to find the underlying cause.
Experts say chapped lips should not be dismissed as a minor issue. Using lip balm regularly, giving up the habit of licking the lips, and avoiding irritating cosmetics can go a long way toward keeping dryness under control.

The anatomy of unrest
item.description:
Severe unrest, including riots and episodes of mob violence, has erupted in several countries, in many cases involving younger people. In that situation, there is a possibility of a broader pattern that deserves our scrutiny. It is absolutely true that global economic stagnation, as well as geopolitical or domestic political instability, has made life difficult for marginalised communities and the middle class in many countries.
But what can explain the fire that engulfed the historic Limoges city hall in France recently, or the bulldozer that vandalised the historic museum on Dhanmondi Road No 32 in Bangladesh, which survived the Pakistani atrocities, the Liberation War, and subsequent military rule?
These events raise questions about whether our collective capacity for restraint is weakening. These acts are not just destructive; they represent collective desecration of civilization, where enraged mobs can turn on anything.
When we see crowds burn what survived world wars and genocidal atrocities, the core issue is no longer their so-called grievances, but what collapse turns them into an instinct for barbarity.
This kind of antagonistic behavioral change may arise from multiple interacting factors, including economic instability, poor living standards, childhood trauma, and digital radicalization amplified by new media algorithms, the normalization of violence, propaganda, fast-paced consumption trends, and even environmental chemical exposure.
Each of these factors plays a role in shaping human behavior, particularly under conditions of social and economic adversity.
In states, from West to East, where policymaking can, under appropriate conditions of course, be done through peaceful discourse and movements, serious violence has erupted instead.
Does this represent a measurable worldwide change in protest, rather than just a series of highly visible episodes?
Even movements with sensible, logical political agendas, such as the quota reform movement in Bangladesh or France’s recent protests demanding reduced military spending in favor of education budgets, resort to widespread violence where peaceful change is possible.
This disconnect suggests that there is something else.
This issue with impulse control isn’t just limited to any specific class of people; it’s a problem affecting the entire nation and subsequently affecting the entire globe. In Bangladesh’s background, after 2024, we are witnessing a society that seems to have no impulse control whatsoever.
Thinking about these things reminds me of Tofazzal Hossain from Dhaka University. So-called “sane” students beat up a mentally ill man until he was half-dead; then, after a brief pause, they fed him rice, and they beat him again. This time, they beat him to death.
Next, I am reminded of Dipu Das. A mob beat him, hung his body from a tree, and burned it, while bystanders cheered, and yet no one thought, “Shouldn’t we stop?”
Absorbing the venom of extremism, a group attacked a shrine in Rajbari, exhumed the body of a man named Nurul Pagla from his grave, and set it on fire simply to express their hatred against Sufis.
These acts are committed by new generation of people who simply do not know how to stop. They keep beating even a lifeless body. A terrifying breakdown of law and order and anarchy has been ongoing in the country since the 2024 political change.
But can that discontinuity of political sanity really explain such raw, brutal violence? But how are these people becoming so monstrous in the first place? People gather quickly there to launch an attack, escalating with the swiftness of a jaguar charging at a stray deer in the jungle.
Immediately, people stand by with their cameras, smiling and ready to record. A widely cited line of research on nonviolent political movements suggests that campaigns mobilising a relatively small proportion of a country’s population, even approximately 3.5 % of the body politic, have historically achieved meaningful political change.
Research by Erica Chenoweth and Maria J. Stephan, studying major resistance campaigns, found that nonviolent campaigns were generally more successful than violent ones in achieving their stated objectives.
However, the 3.5% threshold should not be interpreted as a universal rule guaranteeing success. It tells about patterns observed in particular historical cases rather than an automatic formula for political transformation, as Chenoweth herself said. Yet violence has erupted in various contexts where mass mobilisation initially came from legitimate grievances or aspirations for peaceful change.
This raises an important question: why do recent movements experience severe escalation or the emergence of violent tactics? Yes, yes, I heard the quote, “when peaceful revolution becomes impossible, violent revolution becomes inevitable.”
But how does that argument apply to protests or mob violence in France, a liberal democracy in Europe, where citizens can openly protest outside the offices of the Prime Minister or President, openly insult their leaders, and publicly denounce government policies without having to resort to violence to make their voices heard?
Recent demonstrations in France, for example, have involved demands concerning school conditions, teacher shortages, declining public services, inequality, and the rising cost of living.
However, within the same demonstrations for stated political agendas, we have seen mobs, sometimes forming the majority of the crowd, attacking businesses and homes, looting, and vandalising. But the existence of violence where peaceful political participation is possible does not, by itself, establish that hidden agendas or organised sponsorship were responsible.
A more rigorous way for us to understand this phenomenon is to distinguish between the legitimacy of a movement’s grievances, the methods through which it mobilises, and the political consequences of its actions. A movement may come from genuine socioeconomic frustration, yet its mobilisation can subsequently be shaped by misinformation, political opportunism, or the intervention of organised actors.
Moreover, the transition from protest to violence should not be treated as an automatic or inevitable outcome of public anger; rather, it is a process that requires its own explanation. Including the role of group dynamics, digital information networks, and actors who seek to exploit or intensify disorder for political or economic gain.
Identifying the beneficiaries of unrest does not, by itself, prove that they orchestrated it, just as establishing the legitimacy of a movement’s grievances does not automatically justify every method employed in its name.
Digital communication adds another dimension to this process. Internet platforms can reduce the cost of mobilisation, accelerate the circulation of information, and enable people to coordinate protests without conventional organisational structures.
However, these same mechanisms and cyber algorithms can reward outrage, amplify sensationalist content, and circulate unverified allegations, creating the impression that extreme positions enjoy greater public support than they actually do.
It can function as a complete gateway to mass violence, even massacre or genocide, which we have seen in Myanmar when social media was literally used as a medium for the Rohingya genocide of 2017 in Rakhine, Myanmar.
A similar example was evident in Bangladesh in 2024 and subsequently in 2025, when social media was used not merely to broadcast and celebrate the vandalism of a museum and the subsequent attacks on the country’s two leading national dailies, but also to facilitate mobilisation and coordination surrounding these incidents.
Just as demands for educational reform and better public services in France do not explain or justify the vandalism. Bangladesh’s 2024 quota-reform movement and broader demands for accountability should not be conflated with the subsequent terror and breakdown of political order.
The circulation of organised propaganda and the celebration of violence further amplify its impact. In many situations, people may not fully understand how to respond to unfolding events that are happening so fast. Once a coordinated response appears and gains momentum, many people may simply follow the prevailing trend without critically thinking about its implications.
Although not every episode of mass violence requires a centrally coordinated conspiracy, this should not obscure the possibility of organised action in specific cases.
Consider the difference between the mobs in France and Bangladesh. Many of the participants in France’s unrest may belong to far-left or anarchist fringes, whose actions, however destructive,may be rooted in an identifiable ideological lineage.
But what ideology, if any, explains the brutality of the mobs in Bangladesh?
Do these mobs even understand the political ideas they might claim to represent?
Or has violence itself become the purpose, with them joining a collective frenzy without fully understanding its motives, consequences, or even its supposed political objectives?
A related but often overlooked dimension of this issue is the potential long-term behavioural impact of environmental neurotoxins, particularly lead.
In his 2007 study, Rick Nevin, an economist who has worked to eliminate childhood lead poisoning, studied the relationship between preschool blood-lead levels and subsequent crime trends across the United States.
He also extended his analysis in Britain, Canada, France, Australia, Finland, Italy, West Germany, and New Zealand. His findings identified a strong statistical association between childhood lead exposure and later trends in violent crime, with time lags consistent with the possibility that early-life neurodevelopmental damage may influence behaviour later in life.
He demonstrated that the rise and fall of violent crime in America completely correlates with the timeframe of adding lead to gasoline, following a more than two-decade time lag.
The correlations were reportedly above 0.9 in the analyses discussed, an unusually high level in the social sciences. Although correlation does not establish causation, the strength and consistency of these associations across multiple countries, combined with the apparent temporal relationship between childhood chemical exposure and later crime trends, make the findings difficult to dismiss outright.
In Bangladesh, childhood exposure to neurotoxic substances includes unregulated lead-acid battery recycling, lead-containing paints, contaminated turmeric, industrial pollution, and arsenic-contaminated groundwater.
The World Health Organization emphasises that no blood-lead concentration is known to be safe and that lead exposure can adversely affect children’s intelligence and behaviour. The Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025 reported that approximately 38% of children aged 12-59 months had blood-lead concentrations at or above 5 micrograms per decilitre (µg/dL).
A 2022-24 study by icddr,b and Stanford University, testing 500 children aged 2 to 4 in Dhaka, found lead in every child’s blood, with 98% exceeding the threshold that the U.S. classifies as requiring “immediate attention.”
Where is this lead coming from?
One of the primary sources is unregulated battery recycling. Over 3 million battery-run rickshaws operate in the country, each using five lead-acid batteries with a lifespan of only 6 to 11 months.
These batteries are melted in open furnaces across more than a thousand unregulated smelting yards (bhattis) scattered nationwide, mostly within residential areas, according to UNEP and Pure Earth data. In the Stanford study, children living within 1 kilometer of such sites had blood lead levels 43% higher than others. But lead isn’t the only poison.
The tanneries of Hazaribagh have submerged generations in chromium, and tens of millions in rural areas have been drinking arsenic-contaminated tubewell water for decades.
A developing brain can barely defend itself against even one of these toxins; when several hit during the same childhood, it stands almost no chance. Now, let us consider whether the approximately two-decade lag identified in Nevin’s research raises questions in the Bangladeshi context.
Most of the individuals committing murder in the 2024-26 mob violence were born in the early 2000s and later.
That was precisely the era when Bangladesh’s vehicle fleet tripled, battery recycling proliferated, and Dhaka’s air, soil, and water were absorbing the very chemicals that icddr,b is only now measuring in the blood of today’s two-year-olds. However, the argument need not depend entirely on the precision of this temporal calculation.
Even if the specific 22-year lag observed in the American context cannot be directly transposed to Bangladesh, the broader question of environmental harm on human behavioral development remains important.
Another critical dimension is the political economy of disorder, as discussed earlier.
Political or socioeconomic instability rarely affects all actors equally. Governments may use disorder to justify exceptional security measures; opposition groups may exploit it to delegitimise incumbents; and businesses may benefit from certain forms of reconstruction expenditure.
Yet the conditions shaping human behaviour begin to develop long before individuals enter the political arena. Persistent poverty, unemployment, financial insecurity, and repeated setbacks impose chronic psychological strain, narrowing attention towards immediate survival and leaving fewer cognitive resources for deliberation and emotional regulation.
Economists Anandi Mani and her colleagues found that financial scarcity can impair cognitive performance, while other research links failures of self-control to aggression, and adverse childhood experiences can affect long-term development.
Under accumulated frustration, humiliation, and perceived deprivation, individuals become more vulnerable to impulsive reactions, particularly when provoked or mobilised by others.
This argument challenges explanations that treat violent behaviour exclusively as a product of ideology, political allegiance, or cultural values.
If environmental conditions can affect emotional regulation and impulse control, and poverty and prolonged adversity can undermine psychological development, then the origins of social behaviour are more complex than conventional political analysis acknowledges.
What appears on the surface as intolerance or an inability to exercise restraint could, in many circumstances, be shaped by developmental, psychological, and environmental factors that have received insufficient attention. This is not to suggest that political beliefs, moral responsibility, or human behaviour can be reduced to brain chemistry.
Rather, biological, psychological, and social-political dimensions may interact, and an adequate explanation of collective violence should not exclude any of them without sufficient evidence.
If we continue to ignore the conditions that make violence easier to unleash while tolerating those who deliberately unleash it, we will remain trapped in a cycle of destruction, addressing its consequences while neglecting its deeper roots.
Tasin Mahdi, an interdisciplinary essayist based in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

item.title: Who will regulate the race for deep-sea resources?
item.description:
The growing race to exploit deep-sea resources is raising concerns over environmental damage, fragmented international oversight and accountability, as countries and companies seek minerals essential for batteries and clean energy technologies.
Polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts and polymetallic sulphides found on the ocean floor contain nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. While these resources could diversify mineral supplies, large-scale extraction could destroy seabed habitats, disturb sediments and threaten poorly understood marine ecosystems.
The central question is who will prevent environmental damage in international waters and hold those responsible accountable when harm occurs.
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) provides the principal legal framework for ocean governance. However, responsibility is divided among institutions overseeing seabed minerals, shipping, fisheries and marine biodiversity, creating challenges in coordinating environmental protection and enforcement.
The International Seabed Authority (ISA) regulates mineral-related activities in the international seabed Area beyond national jurisdiction. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) develops international standards for shipping safety and pollution prevention, while the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) supports sustainable fisheries management.
Although these institutions have distinct mandates, their activities can affect the same marine ecosystems. The combined effects of mining, shipping and fishing may remain difficult to assess when environmental data and monitoring systems are fragmented.
An activity could comply with one regulatory framework while contributing to environmental pressures that another institution does not adequately address. Establishing responsibility for damage becomes particularly difficult when several operators and regulatory systems are involved.
The Agreement on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, known as the BBNJ Agreement or High Seas Treaty, entered into force on January 17, 2026.
The agreement establishes a framework for marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments, marine genetic resources and benefit-sharing, alongside capacity-building and technology transfer.
However, it does not replace the separate legal arrangements governing international seabed mining, shipping or fisheries. Coordination among existing institutions remains essential.
Effective implementation will require credible environmental assessments, transparent information-sharing, scientific monitoring and action against violations. The treaty's entry into force does not automatically guarantee effective conservation.
The challenge is particularly significant for developing countries, which often lack the research vessels, seabed sensors, specialised equipment and analytical capacity needed to independently monitor activities in distant international waters.
Without reliable baseline data and continuous monitoring, determining whether environmental changes result from a particular activity, natural processes, or other human pressures can be difficult.
Unequal access to scientific research and technology can also limit developing countries' ability to challenge environmental claims and participate meaningfully in international negotiations.
For Bangladesh, the issue is closely connected to the health of the Bay of Bengal, fisheries, coastal livelihoods and the country's blue economy.
The Bangladesh Oceanographic Research Institute (BORI) is conducting research on coastal marine resources, potential fishing habitats and marine pollution.
Abu Sharif Md Mahabub E Kibria, a marine scientist at BORI working on environmental and climate issues, said the institute was researching potentially valuable mineral resources along the coast, identifying potential fish habitats and detecting marine pollution in coastal and adjacent areas.
BORI is also working on extracting agar and carrageenan from seaweed and identifying suitable areas for seaweed cultivation in the sea.
These activities could strengthen Bangladesh's understanding of marine resources and environmental changes. However, coastal mineral exploration and mining in the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction involve different geographical areas, legal frameworks and environmental conditions.
Bangladesh's exclusive economic zone is legally distinct from international waters, where the country does not automatically exercise direct regulatory control. Nevertheless, marine pollution and ecological changes can cross maritime boundaries, affecting fisheries, food security and coastal economies.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Department of Fisheries and BORI could play important roles in monitoring international developments, strengthening scientific research and representing Bangladesh's interests in global negotiations.
Expanding access to marine data, developing research partnerships and improving technical expertise would help Bangladesh assess emerging risks and advocate for stronger environmental safeguards and fairer access to marine genetic resources.
Ultimately, the race for deep-sea resources cannot be governed by a single treaty or institution. Effective oversight will depend on coordination among regulatory bodies, transparent environmental assessments, reliable scientific evidence and clear procedures for investigating violations.
The challenge is not simply determining who can extract resources from the deep sea, but ensuring that economic benefits are shared fairly, environmental damage is prevented wherever possible and those responsible are held accountable.
Earlier, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said: "International cooperation and effective implementation of the BBNJ Agreement are important for protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction."
Then again, Leticia Carvalho, the ISA secretary-general, said: "Environmental protection, scientific evidence and effective regulatory oversight are central to governing international seabed mineral activities."
Even, Qu Dongyu, director-general of FAO, said: "Sustainable fisheries management requires science-based decisions, responsible harvesting and action against illegal fishing."
Expressing his opinion to Dhaka Tribune, Professor Ainun Nishat, an environmental and water resources expert, said: "Decisions on deep-sea resource extraction should account for environmental impacts, scientific evidence and long-term risks rather than economic potential alone."
Energy and environmental specialist Professor Ijaz Hossain from Buet, said: "Demand for minerals used in clean energy technologies should be considered alongside alternatives, recycling and safeguards against additional environmental damage."
Talking to Dhaka Tribune, Abu Sharif Md Mahabub E Kibria, marine scientist at BORI, said: "BORI is researching potential coastal mineral resources, fish habitats, marine pollution, seaweed-derived agar and carrageenan, and suitable areas for seaweed cultivation."
University of Dhaka oceanography and fisheries researchers and BORI marine scientists agreed that long-term research and regular monitoring are needed to assess deep-sea biodiversity and ecosystem risks, where scientific information remains limited; besides, scientific data and regional cooperation are important for understanding how changes in international waters could affect marine species, food webs and fisheries.

item.title: 21 BGB platoons deployed for Thakurgaon-1 by-election
item.description:
Twenty-one platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in the Thakurgaon-1 constituency ahead of the by-election to help ensure a free, fair and peaceful vote.
BGB personnel have been on duty in the constituency since Sunday, according to Thakurgaon Battalion (50 BGB).
The troops have been deployed across three upazilas, 22 unions and one municipality within the constituency. They will operate as mobile units and striking forces in their assigned areas.
Intelligence operations have also been intensified to strengthen security. At a press briefing, BGB officials said personnel were using body-worn cameras and drones to monitor key locations.
The force said its primary objective was to ensure that voters could cast their ballots safely and without obstruction.
Officials said BGB personnel are also monitoring the situation to ensure candidates have equal opportunities to campaign and that the electoral code of conduct is followed.
The force remains on alert to prevent unrest, violence and other activities that could threaten public safety during the election. Surveillance and patrols have also been strengthened in border areas.

item.title: Writ filed seeking halt to illegal sand extraction from Padma
item.description:
A writ petition has been filed with the High Court seeking to stop illegal and unplanned sand extraction from the Padma River, citing concerns over riverbank erosion, environmental damage and the safety of the Padma Bridge and its associated infrastructure.
Dr Md Golam Rahman Bhuiyan, chairman of human rights and social development organisation Manobadhikar O Samaj Unnayan Sangstha (MOSUS), filed the public interest petition on Monday. He is also a lawyer and human rights activist.
The petition raises concerns that illegal, unplanned sand extraction could alter the river's natural course, weaken its banks, and damage the surrounding environment and biodiversity. It also warns of potential risks to important national infrastructure, including the Padma Bridge.
It seeks High Court directives requiring the relevant government authorities to fulfil their legal responsibilities, investigate allegations of illegal sand extraction, take legal action against those responsible and implement effective measures to prevent further violations.
The Padma River plays a vital role in Bangladesh's economy, environment, agriculture and fisheries, as well as in the livelihoods of communities along its banks. Disruptions to its natural flow and ecological balance could threaten agricultural land, natural resources and the people who depend on the river.
The petition also highlights the need for scientific assessments and regular monitoring to evaluate the potential impact of sand extraction on the river and the safety of the Padma Bridge and related infrastructure.
MOSUS said the relevant authorities must take effective steps to protect natural resources, uphold environmental justice and ensure the rule of law.
Through the public interest litigation, the organisation seeks judicial intervention to ensure that the authorities take lawful and effective measures to protect the Padma River.

item.title: PM arrives in Tokyo on four-day state visit to Japan
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman arrived in Tokyo on Monday morning on a four-day state visit to Japan at the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
A Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight carrying the prime minister, his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and other members of the entourage landed at Narita International Airport at 9:05am local time, according to the Prime Minister's Office.
At the airport, the prime minister was received by Japanese State Minister for Foreign Affairs Yasutaka Nakasone.
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Rehan Asif Asad, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Overseas Employment in the Asia-Pacific Region Shakirul Islam Khan and senior officials of the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo were also present.
He was later taken to the Imperial Hotel, where he will stay during the visit, in a ceremonial motorcade.
Earlier, the flight departed from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 12:10am Bangladesh time.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Prime Minister’s Political Adviser and BNP acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, Chief Whip Nurul Islam Moni and Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Ghani saw the Prime Minister and his wife off at the VIP lounge of the Dhaka airport.
The prime minister is leading a small delegation during the visit.
The delegation includes Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Finance and Planning Adviser Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, Invest Bangladesh Authority Executive Chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun, Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam, Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury and Economic Relations Division Secretary Md Shahriar Kader Siddiky.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi are scheduled to hold a high-level formal meeting on Tuesday morning.
A joint declaration will be issued after the meeting.
Later, the prime minister and members of his delegation will attend a luncheon hosted by the Japanese prime minister.
During the visit, Tarique Rahman will hold talks with Japanese government officials, development institutions and business leaders, visit industrial and energy facilities, and deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum.
The visit is expected to deepen the existing strategic partnership, attract fresh Japanese investment, expand trade and accelerate ongoing development projects, said Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam while speaking at a curtain-raiser media briefing at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on October 20.
Discussions will focus on the effective implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement.
The two sides will also explore wider cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.
The prime minister’s tentative programmes include engagements with the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League and the chairman of the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation.
Meetings are also being planned with the president of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), the president of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and the chairman of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation.
The foreign secretary said the two sides are discussing draft memoranda of understanding (MoU) and cooperation agreements covering agriculture, fisheries, human resource development, skills enhancement, civil aviation, trade, environmental conservation and local government modernisation.
"We hope that many of these MoUs will be signed during the visit," he said.
Around eight MoUs are under discussion, of which three to four could be signed during the visit. Separate agreements are also being pursued in education and human resource development.
Detailed discussions are planned on Japanese support for establishing factories in Bangladesh, generating employment and developing human resources in line with the prime minister's priorities.
The two sides are also expected to discuss regional and international peace and stability, a sustainable and peaceful solution to the Rohingya crisis, stronger cooperation in addressing the energy crisis and efforts to end international conflicts.
The visit follows the prime minister's participation in an online meeting in April at the invitation of the Japanese prime minister, during which Bangladesh welcomed a Japan-led initiative to address energy challenges across Asia.

item.title: NBR raids Gulshan restaurant, seizes alcohol over suspected duty evasion
item.description:
A joint team of four intelligence agencies of the National Board of Revenue (NBR) seized a large quantity of alcohol and alcoholic beverages without valid documents during a raid on Kingfisher Restaurant Ltd in the capital’s Gulshan area.
The special operation was conducted from 12:30am on Sunday and continued for around three hours, following confidential information received by the NBR that highly dutiable goods, particularly alcohol and alcoholic beverages, are being procured and sold by evading duties.
The operation was carried out under the NBR’s directives and the overall supervision of the Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID), according to a press release issued on Monday.
The participating agencies were the Central Intelligence Cell (CIC), CIID, Tax Intelligence and Investigation Unit (TIIU), and VAT Audit, Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (VAIID).
The team conducted the raid to identify stocks of alcohol allegedly obtained through illegal sources and smuggling, prevent value-added tax (VAT) evasion on local sales, verify whether sales proceeds had been properly declared in income tax returns, and examine possible links between the transactions and money laundering.
The operation was conducted under the provisions of the Customs Act, 2023, the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012, the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Rules, 2016, and the Income Tax Act, 2023.
The Special Response Battalion (SRB-1) provided support throughout the operation.
The NBR did not specify the quantity or estimated value of the seized alcohol in its press release issued on Monday.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 4th among world's most polluted cities Monday morning
item.description:
Dhaka ranked as the world's fourth most polluted city on Monday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 168 at 9:30am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", indicating that the concentration of airborne pollutants had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general public, according to the AQI scale.
India's Delhi topped the list with an AQI score of 200, followed by Pakistan's Lahore and Karachi, with scores of 199 and 175, respectively.
An AQI reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while a score between 151 and 200 is classified as "unhealthy". Readings between 201 and 300 are deemed "very unhealthy", and levels above 301 are considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI, an index that tracks daily air quality, indicates how polluted the air is and the potential health effects on residents.
In Bangladesh, AQI measurements are based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and ozone.
According to the World Health Organization, air pollution causes an estimated seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

Carrick on the brink as Utd misery mounts, Isak stars for Liverpool
item.description:
Michael Carrick was pushed to the brink of being sacked after Manchester United slumped to a miserable 3-0 home defeat against Bournemouth, while Alexander Isak extended his hot streak in Liverpool's 2-0 win against Brighton on Sunday.
Carrick's bold decision to drop captain Bruno Fernandes backfired as defeat stretched United's winless run to eight games and left them 16th in the Premier League, just one point above the relegation zone.
For the third time in four seasons, the Cherries won by a three-goal margin at Old Trafford as strikes from Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson secured a fully deserved victory for Marco Rose's side.
Fernandes was critical of Carrick's tactics in a 4-1 Champions League thrashing at Como on Wednesday.
The United boss said the decision to leave out last season's Premier League Player of the Year was a "purely football" driven, but it was hard to believe Fernandes was not being punished as he was left on the bench for the entire match.
Carrick was taunted with chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning" from the Bournemouth fans.
But on this evidence, dismissing another manager is far from a quick fix for a club that has fallen dramatically from grace since Alex Ferguson's retirement after winning their most recent English title 13 years ago.
A strong finish to last season during Carrick's interim spell in charge secured third place in the Premier League.
Yet with just one win against promoted Ipswich, United have taken just seven points from eight league games so far this season -- their lowest tally at this stage of a season since 1986-87.
United's players were booed off by the few frustrated fans that remained inside Old Trafford at the end of their heaviest home defeat since 2024.
United's co-owners the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe were also targeted for angry chants, although Carrick largely avoided the fans' ire.
It is unlikely that sympathy vote will spare the former United midfielder from the axe.
At Anfield, Liverpool struck twice in quick succession in the first half, with Pascal Gross's own goal followed by Isak's latest strike.
Isak has netted six times in seven league games this season and has three goals in his last four matches.
After a turbulent debut season following his acrimonious move from Newcastle, the Sweden striker is finally beginning to repay his £125 million ($167 million) fee.
It was a welcome first taste of top-flight success at Anfield for Reds boss Andoni Iraola, who had failed to win his first three league games on Merseyside since arriving from Bournemouth in the close season.
The Spaniard, who had won Champions League and League Cup games at Anfield, has led Liverpool to four successive victories in all competitions since the chastening 3-0 home defeat against Manchester City.
Liverpool have climbed to fourth place, just one point behind third-placed Brighton after inflicting the high-flying Seagulls' second league loss this term.
The rampant Reds are six points behind leaders City as they eye a potential title challenge.
William Osula and Harvey Barnes scored in the second half as Newcastle piled pressure on Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage with a 2-0 win at Selhurst Park.
Thrashed 5-0 at rivals Brighton last weekend, 17th-placed Palace have won just twice in eight league games under Sage, who arrived from Lens in the close season to replace Oliver Glasner.
Hull's unbeaten home record remains intact but the Tigers have not tasted victory for seven games after a 1-1 draw with Brentford at the MKM Stadium.
Oli McBurnie's 24th-minute penalty, awarded when Aaron Hickey fouled Tim Iroegbunam, put Hull ahead, but Dango Ouattara equalised in the 63rd minute.

item.title: Mbappe double helps Real stun Barca in La Liga Clasico
item.description:
Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid a 2-1 Clasico victory over La Liga leaders Barcelona on Sunday at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points.
French superstar Mbappe opened the scoring before the interval and then slotted home late on to inflict Barca's first domestic defeat of the campaign after Raphinha had equalised for the champions.
Real Madrid remain third, behind Atletico Madrid and Hansi Flick's Barca, who had won their first nine games before a chastening week.
The Catalans suffered a second straight defeat after losing on Tuesday against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League.
Mourinho was delighted with his team's display in his first Clasico back at the helm of Madrid.
"My team had an extraordinary game, very organised, good concentration, with courage to play out from the back against a team that presses you a lot," Mourinho told reporters.
"We had chances for the second goal... obviously Barca had a strong reaction but we were calm and organised and at 1-1 we never lost our tranquility."
Barca had won six of the seven previous Clasicos since Flick arrived but were surprisingly subdued against Mourinho's side.
"You saw today, we lacked freshness," said Flick of his team's performance.
"It's the first defeat in La Liga, we won nine in a row. This is what we have to see.
"Defeats are a part of the game. We have to analyse, we have to make things better. Now it's important that we make a reaction."
Los Blancos, without suspended winger Vinicius Junior, won their fifth straight game across all competitions and are finding their footing under veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho.
After two trophyless seasons Madrid turned back to Mourinho to try and stop Barca's dominance, and this result will give them hope they are on the right track.
The opening period of the game was cagey, with few opportunities.
Barca defender Pau Cubarsi twice reacted well to shut down Mbappe, while Real Madrid's Marc Cucurella took a rapid liking for Lamine Yamal's shirt, constantly grabbing at the 19-year-old winger.
Anthony Gordon, playing in his first Clasico since joining Barcelona from Newcastle, backheeled the ball to Raphinha, who fired narrowly wide as Barca threatened.
The hosts were dealt a setback when young defender Xavi Espart pulled up hurt and needed to be replaced by Alejandro Balde before the half-hour mark.
Andriy Lunin, playing in goal for Madrid after Thibaut Courtois pulled out of the squad with flu, saved at his near post from Gordon before the visitors took the lead.
Mbappe scored his 10th league goal of the season and also his easiest, with Barca's Gerard Martin clearing a cross straight at the Frenchman, who deflected it into the net.
Barca responded by carving out a glorious chance for an equaliser but teenage sensation Yamal for once miscued in front of goal, firing wide when poised to level.
The game opened up and Yan Diomande came close to doubling Madrid's lead before half-time, drilling into the side-netting.
Martin redeemed himself early in the second half as he held off Jude Bellingham, who could neither beat the defender nor find a free Mbappe.
Raphinha, who had a quiet first half, pulled Barcelona level just after the hour mark.
Pedri fed the Brazilian, La Liga's top goalscorer with 13, who fired through Bellingham's legs and Lunin could not keep the shot out.
The Ukrainian goalkeeper did make a superb save to deny Martin at a corner, as Barcelona flowed forward with the wind finally in their sails.
Yamal bent an effort wide with Lunin at full stretch and Barca substitute Frenkie de Jong had a shot desperately blocked by Dean Huijsen.
There was a sting in the tail for the Catalans though as substitute Gabriel Jesus lost possession and Madrid raced through on goal.
Eduardo Camavinga beat Cubarsi and unselfishly cut the ball back for Mbappe to tuck home his second of the night into an empty net with Joan Garcia drawn out of position.
It brought up a century of goals since Mbappe joined Madrid from PSG in 2024, although the trophies to match have not yet followed.
"(Winning) is a good message today, but we can't think the season is done -- next week (at Racing) Santander we have to put in the same intensity," Mbappe told Real Madrid TV.

item.title: Govt issues ordinance for solar power systems up to 5MW
item.description:
The government has issued an ordinance regulating the installation, operation and approval of solar power systems with a capacity of up to 5 megawatts (MW).
The ordinance allows solar installations at public and private institutions, residential buildings, industrial facilities, tea gardens, irrigation pumps, cold storage facilities and electric vehicle charging stations. However, large-scale ground-mounted solar power projects are excluded from its scope.
It also prescribes penalties for obstructing solar power installation or damaging solar facilities.
The president promulgated the Special Solar Power Installation Ordinance, 2026 on October 19, introducing provisions on investment, service provider selection, electricity bill adjustments, public procurement and project implementation.
Under the ordinance, priority will be given to the operating expenditure (OPEX) model, under which service providers will finance, install, operate and maintain solar power systems. Payments will be adjusted against the electricity generated in accordance with contractual terms.
Institutions with their own funds or regular income may opt for the capital expenditure (CAPEX) model, financing the installation themselves and retaining ownership of the systems.
The ordinance also requires the relevant authority to prepare and maintain district-wise lists of eligible service providers.
Customers will select providers through a competitive process from the approved lists.
However, they may also appoint providers outside the lists through open tenders to install solar power systems.
The ordinance requires a tripartite agreement among the customer, service provider and relevant authority for project implementation. The agreement will cover equipment quality, safety, installation and maintenance, electricity distribution, the customer’s share of generated power, pricing and payment terms.
It must also include provisions for the safe disposal of expired equipment and e-waste, as well as the return of unusable components.
Special provisions have been introduced for government procurement. Under the CAPEX model, the ceiling for procuring goods and related services through a limited tender has been set at Tk5 crore. The use of electronic government procurement (e-GP) will not be mandatory for procurement under the ordinance. It also includes special provisions on contract approval and duration.
The ordinance allows consumers to use solar-generated electricity to meet their own demand and supply surplus power to the national grid through net metering.
Electricity supplied to the grid will be adjusted against the consumer’s bill for the relevant billing period. If any surplus remains after the adjustment, the consumer will be paid according to applicable rules and government-approved tariffs. The government may also introduce incentives to promote net metering.
A National Policy Council, chaired by the prime minister, will be formed to provide policy guidance on solar power development. It will include ministers or state ministers from the ministries of power, energy and mineral resources, finance and law, as well as secretaries of relevant ministries and representatives of government agencies.
The council will review progress towards renewable energy targets, coordination among agencies, net metering, incentives and the implementation of investment models.
The ordinance also provides for technical and coordination committees at the district and upazila levels. The committees will assist and oversee project implementation, resolve disputes, maintain necessary records and provide training to consumers.
Relevant authorities will also be required to maintain data on solar power systems and regularly monitor whether the installations remain operational.
The ordinance prescribes penalties for stealing solar power systems or their components, trading in stolen components, damaging installations, making illegal connections and obstructing installation or maintenance work.
Stealing or trading in stolen components may result in up to three years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to Tk50,000, or both.
Damaging a solar power installation may carry a maximum penalty of five years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to Tk5 lakh, or both.
Illegal connections and obstructing installation activities may each be punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to Tk5 lakh, or both.
The ordinance has taken immediate effect. The government may issue rules, gazettes, orders and guidelines to facilitate its implementation and provide necessary interpretations.

Winter vegetables arrive in Rajshahi, but prices remain high
item.description:
Early winter vegetables have started arriving in Rajshahi’s wholesale and retail markets, but high prices continue to put pressure on consumers.
A visit to Saheb Bazar Mashtarpatti kitchen market on Sunday morning found a growing variety of winter vegetables, though many remained beyond the reach of ordinary buyers.
Pui shak was selling for Tk10 per kg, while red amaranth and potatoes cost Tk20, papaya Tk25, pointed gourd, taro and elephant foot yam Tk40, onions Tk45, and radish and spiny gourd Tk50 per kg.
Okra and taro stems were selling for Tk60 per kg, while yardlong beans, bitter gourd and cucumber cost Tk70. White eggplant and cauliflower were priced at Tk80 per kg.
Red eggplant and garlic were selling for Tk100 per kg, while green chillies and carrots cost Tk120, beans Tk140, and ginger and tomatoes Tk160. Green bananas were priced at Tk30 for four, while each bottle gourd cost Tk30.
Consumer Anwar Hossain said prices had yet to fall despite the arrival of winter vegetables. Although some items were relatively cheap, the high prices of others made it difficult for consumers to buy a variety of vegetables at once.
Vegetable trader Alauddin said supplies had not increased enough to bring prices down. He expected prices to fall as more produce reached the markets.
Meanwhile, farmers in Paba upazila are expanding early-season vegetable cultivation to take advantage of higher prices before regular winter supplies arrive.
Mosharraf Hossain, a farmer in Paba, said early-season cultivation involved risks, including the potential loss of around 2,000 cauliflower or cabbage plants per bigha. However, farmers could earn substantial profits if they brought their produce to market on time.
He said he had sold cauliflower grown on three bighas and cabbage grown on four-and-a-half bighas at Tk60-70 per head, with prices sometimes reaching Tk90. After deducting production costs, he earned around Tk150,000 per bigha. He is now cultivating cabbage on another 25 bighas.
Another farmer, Nazrul Islam of Alimganj, has grown 4,000 early-season cabbage plants on 12 kathas of land at a cost of Tk18,000-20,000. He has already sold 200 heads at Tk30 each and expects to earn around Tk100,000 from the remaining crop, with a projected profit of Tk80,000 after expenses.
Nazrul said he had earned around Tk500,000 by growing tomatoes on five bighas last year. This season, following advice from the agriculture department, he has planted early-season tomatoes on 10 kathas.
Early-season cauliflower, cabbage, beans, radishes, carrots, eggplants, bottle gourds and leafy vegetables are being cultivated in several areas of Paba, including Haripur, Harian, Damkura, Parila, Borgaichi, Naohata and Paikpara.
Paba Upazila Agriculture Officer MA Mannan said the upazila had already met its seasonal target of cultivating vegetables on 1,895 hectares, with early-season varieties accounting for a significant share.
He said farmers were being encouraged to grow early-season vegetables and advised to use biological pesticides, applying chemical pesticides only at approved doses.
Mustafa Kamal Hossain, deputy director of the Department of Agricultural Extension in Rajshahi, said the district had set a target of cultivating vegetables on 6,430 hectares this season. Early-season vegetable cultivation had increased by 200 hectares compared with previous years, he added.

item.title: Ex-MP Abdul Mannan sent to jail in anti-terrorism case
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Sunday ordered former Meherpur-1 MP Professor Abdul Mannan to be sent to jail after rejecting his bail petition in an anti-terrorism case.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ariful Islam passed the order, said SI Arif Reza of the prosecution department.
Earlier on Sunday, Detective Branch (DB) police arrested Abdul Mannan from his residence in Dhanmondi at around 6am.
Investigation officer Inspector Md Masudur Rahman of the Tejgaon Zonal Team produced him before the court and sought an order to keep him in jail. Lawyer Al Imran Mukul, representing Abdul Mannan, sought bail, while the prosecution opposed the application.
After the hearing, the court rejected the bail petition and ordered him to be sent to jail. However, Abdul Mannan was not produced in the courtroom during the hearing.
According to the case statement, on the morning of June 18, 35-40 leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and Bangladesh Chhatra League, including Nibas Majumder, brought out a procession near Mohakhali Bus Terminal under the jurisdiction of Tejgaon Industrial Area police station.
The allegations state that the procession involved anti-government slogans and crude bomb explosions, causing panic among the public and involving anti-state activities.
On the same day, Sub-Inspector Mohammad Zahidul Haque of Tejgaon Industrial Area police station filed the case.

item.title: President stresses improved textile education to reduce reliance on foreign experts
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Sunday stressed the need to improve textile education and research to produce internationally competitive engineers and specialists and reduce the sector’s dependence on foreign experts.
He made the remarks when a seven-member delegation led by Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX) Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Md Julhas Uddin paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban.
Describing textiles as one of the country’s major economic sectors, the president emphasised ensuring suitable employment opportunities at home and abroad for textile graduates.
This would help make proper use of the country’s skilled human resources while earning foreign currency, he said, underscoring the need to increase domestic cotton production to meet the raw material requirements of the textile industry.
He called for taking steps to encourage farmers, explore ways to reduce production costs and strengthen coordination between the agriculture and textile sectors.
He further stressed the need for more research into extracting fibres from natural sources, including jute, pineapple leaves and banana plants, alongside the development of synthetic yarn.
During the meeting, the delegation briefed the president on BUTEX’s contributions to the development of the country’s textile and readymade garment industries, as well as its academic and research activities.
They also highlighted several issues requiring attention, including infrastructure development, the establishment of modern laboratories, recruitment of additional staff, the creation of a separate BCS (Textile) cadre, increased budgetary allocations and the allocation of land in Purbachal, Dhaka, for a second campus.
The president listened to their concerns and advised them to contact the relevant ministries to resolve the issues. He also assured the delegation of his cooperation.
During the meeting, the VC invited the president, also the chancellor of the university, to preside over BUTEX’s second convocation, scheduled for March next year.
The president accepted the invitation and assured the delegation that he would attend the event.

item.description:
The government has now appointed BNP leader Dr Sahadat Hossain, who became the mayor of Chittagong City Corporation (CCC) following a court verdict, as the full-time administrator of the same city corporation.
The Local Government Division issued a notification on Sunday in this regard.
According to the notification, he will remain in the position until the city corporation is constituted or until further orders are issued.
He will exercise the powers and perform the duties of the city corporation's mayor under Section 4(3) of the Local Government (City Corporation) Amendment Act, 2026.
Sahadat will receive a monthly honorarium and other allowances as prescribed by the rules, the notification added.
Sahadat had filed a case seeking cancellation of the results of the CCC election held on January 27, 2021.
On October 1, 2024, a Chittagong court declared him the winner of the election after hearing his case.
On August 19, 2024, the interim government removed then CCC Mayor Rezaul Karim Chowdhury after the fall of the Awami League government on August 5 in the face of a mass upsurge.
Later, Divisional Commissioner Tofayel Islam was appointed as the CCC administrator.

item.title: Abbasi receives legal notice over derogatory remarks on journalists
item.description:
A legal notice has been sent to Islamic preacher Mufti Dr Syed Muhammad Enayetullah Abbasi, demanding an unconditional apology within seven days for his derogatory remarks about journalists and alleged threats to beat them.
Supreme Court lawyer Khademul Islam issued the notice on Sunday on behalf of Azharul Islam Sujon, an executive committee member of the Court Reporters Unity, an organisation of journalists covering lower courts.
Advocate Khademul Islam confirmed the matter, saying legal action would be taken if Abbasi failed to withdraw his remarks and apologise within seven days of receiving the notice.
The notice said Abbasi made the remarks at an annual religious sermon and prayer gathering at Nishchintapur Hafizia Madrasa in Matlab upazila of Chandpur on October 19.
During the event, he reportedly described Bangladeshi journalists as the worst and said they should be “beaten like dogs”.
He also accused journalists of practising yellow journalism, failing to report positively on a state minister’s alleged efforts to dismantle a drug syndicate, and receiving funding from foreign intelligence agencies. He further alleged that they did not want Bangladesh to prosper.
According to the notice, the remarks amounted to defamatory statements, threats of assault and incitement, creating an atmosphere of fear and insecurity for journalists.
The notice warned that legal action would be pursued under applicable laws if Abbasi failed to comply with the demand for an apology.
